newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech rail strike ends but trouble could lie ahead.
newsitem.headline: Czech rail strike ends but trouble could lie ahead.

text.p: Czech trains began rolling again on Sunday after unions called off a five-day-old national strike but signals show further labour problems could be down the track.

Union leaders and government representatives reached agreement late on Saturday to end the stoppage, which has crippled the national network and worried businesses dependent on rail freight, after a marathon six hours of talks.

"Now the future will show whether we have reached a compromise which will be perceived by everybody as the maximum possible," CTK news agency quoted Association of Unions of Railway Workers (OSZ) chairman Jaromir Dusek as saying.
Rail traffic all over the Czech Republic began to run normally after the strike ended at midnight (2300 GMT), CTK news agency reported.
"There are no winners and losers. There are only people who will pay for the strike," Transport Minister Martin Riman told Czech Television on Sunday.

The strike, which began on Tuesday and was originally intended to last just 48 hours, was called to demand a rethink of government plans to reform the creaking rail system which could have cost tens of thousands of jobs.

Under the compromise deal, the transport ministry agreed to come up with a new transport strategy by May 31. The rail unions, which represent the network's 101,000 employees, would be consulted on the plans, CTK said.
The strike was the first major confrontation between the government and unions since the 1989 fall of communism, but the threat of more public sector unrest remains.
Teachers began daily selective strikes last month, closing schools across the country and deep discontent in the debt-stricken health service has led to threats of stoppages.

The centre-right government of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus has resisted public sector demands which might threaten its international reputation for fiscal prudence. The budget was one billion crowns in deficit in 1996 after running a surpus for three successive years.
But political analyst Jiri Pehe of the Open Media Research Institute said the government, lauded for its pro-market reforms, had failed to undertake necssary reforms in the public sector.
"Klaus has been very successful at privatising the economy...but the public sector has suffered. It is not so much a question of budget as of lack of restructuring."
Pehe said Klaus, whose government lost its parliamentary majority in last June's elections, had missed an opportunity.

"Instead of taking some difficult decisions and going on wirth streamlining or liberalising prices, they waited and now they are really trapped. All these things are coming back at them like boomerangs," he said.
Deputy Prime Minister Josef Lux, who played a key role in the talks to end the rail strike, acknowledged on Sunday that reform of the network was "still waiting to happen."
The strike also highlighted strains within the ruling coalition, dominated by Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS).
Lux, who heads the junior Christian Democratic Union (KDU-CSL) and is often seen as a potential rival for the premiership, was quoted as saying he had been invited to mediate.
Industry Minister Vladimir Dlouhy of the Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA) rejected this in favour of joint negotiations.
